narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 54.9% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, that is slightly more likely to fail than to pass—not a certainty, but enough for the school to treat the application as high-risk.

Of the factors that most influenced that estimate, your third-year class standing was the strongest. At 6, it was slightly above the average for accepted students (5.79), so it actually pushed the prediction toward passing. The next most important factor, however, was your LSAT score. At 32.5, it was below the accepted-student average of 37.18, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. The third most important factor was your first-year class standing. At 4, it was well below the accepted-student average of 6, and it also pushed toward failure. Together, these two weaker academic signals outweighed the favorable signal from your third-year standing and produced the 54.9% failure estimate.

Next, ask admissions whether the decision can be reviewed and what would strengthen a future application. Consider retaking the LSAT if you can improve your score, and document a concrete bar-readiness plan through prep courses, structured study, and academic support. If you reapply, show upward momentum and address the first-year and standardized-test concerns directly.
